title: Minimum-Link Path in 2D
formal:
Does there exist a single deterministic algorithm \(A\) in the real-RAM model specified below and a function \(T:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that, for every valid planar polygonal-domain input \((P,s,t)\) with \(n\) boundary vertices, \(A\) outputs a minimum-link polygonal path from \(s\) to \(t\) contained in \(P\), using at most \(T(n)\) operations, and
\[
\forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:
\qquad T(n)\le\eta n^2?
\]
The source's word “subquadratic” is interpreted here literally as \(o(n^2)\). The target permits logarithmic-factor savings and does not require a fixed power saving \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\).
why: The number of straight portions of a route captures the cost of changing direction, independently of how far the route travels. This question asks whether exact optimization of that basic geometric objective can avoid a quadratic operation count in environments with many obstacles, where the planar Euclidean shortest-path objective has a different complexity.
status_note: Source-open under an explicitly documented literal o(n²), deterministic real-RAM interpretation. TOPP Problem 22 labels the question open in its 2 August 2001 entry. The individual source review and bounded later-work search on 16 September 2026 found no matching exact planar resolution; 3SUM-hardness is conditional evidence and does not refute this little-o target, especially given known logarithmic-factor improvements for 3SUM itself. The 2025 Dagstuhl report concerns the approximation frontier. This status is not a claim of an exhaustive current-openness check.

progress.text: An exact planar algorithm with nearly quadratic worst-case real-arithmetic operation count is published.
TOPP records the subquadratic question as open; this is the entry’s listed revision date.
The preprint of Minimum-Link Paths Revisited proves 3SUM-hardness of unrestricted planar link distance and a subquadratic approximation algorithm.
Revision 3 of Grønlund–Pettie gives a deterministic \(o(n^2)\)-time algorithm for real-number 3SUM; a 3SUM-hardness label cannot by itself rule out literal \(o(n^2)\) time.
Kostitsyna and coauthors separate the boundary-bend and three-dimensional hardness results from unrestricted planar minimum-link paths.
The Dagstuhl seminar concludes with a recorded question about improving subquadratic approximation for unrestricted planar minimum-link paths.

sentences: A minimum-link path connects two given points through closed planar free space while using the fewest straight segments.
The environment may contain many polygonal holes, and the path may bend at arbitrary interior or boundary points and use arbitrary directions.
The question asks for one exact deterministic algorithm whose worst-case real-RAM operation count divided by the square of the total boundary size tends to zero.
This interpretation includes logarithmic-factor savings, and known 3SUM-hardness does not by itself rule them out.
The checked approximation results and hardness results for boundary bends or three-dimensional paths do not settle this planar exact-path target.

definitions:
A closed simple polygonal region is the bounded region enclosed by a non-self-intersecting polygonal cycle, together with its boundary. The input gives an optional closed simple outer polygon \(B\), and finitely many closed simple polygonal obstacle regions \(O_1,\ldots,O_h\). When the outer polygon is absent, set \(B=\mathbb R^2\). Each obstacle is contained in \(B\), their interiors are pairwise disjoint, and the free space is
\[
P=B\setminus\bigcup_{i=1}^{h}\operatorname{int}(O_i).
\]
The input is promised to have connected free space. Boundary contact between obstacles, or with the outer polygon, is allowed; it does not prohibit a path from using the remaining closed free space. The two specified points \(s,t\) belong to \(P\). There is no general-position promise: collinearities, boundary endpoints and tangencies are included. Each polygon is supplied as its cyclic list of real-coordinate vertices, with polygon lengths and delimiters, and \(s,t\) as coordinate pairs. The size \(n\) is the sum of the lengths of all polygon lists, including the outer polygon when present. Neither a triangulation, visibility graph nor preprocessed data structure is supplied.

A polygonal path is a finite list \(q_0,\ldots,q_k\in\mathbb R^2\), where \(q_0=s\), \(q_k=t\), and every closed line segment \([q_{i-1},q_i]\) lies in \(P\). Its number of links is \(k\); the one-point path has zero links and is available when \(s=t\). The required output attains the minimum of \(k\) over all these paths. All intermediate points may lie anywhere in \(P\), including its interior and boundary, and segments may have any orientation. Output consists of the full list of points with exact coordinates in real registers. Obstacle vertices are not the only permitted bends. Because \(P\) is closed, touching an obstacle or following its boundary is permitted, but entering its interior is forbidden.

For this card, a real RAM is a uniform finite program with exact real registers and random-access memory, together with integer control registers and addresses of \(w=c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed program-dependent integer \(c\ge1\). A real-register copy, an input/output operation on a register, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, square root of a nonnegative real, and comparison of two reals each cost one operation. Word reads, writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic each cost one operation; addition, subtraction and multiplication are modulo \(2^w\), integer division by a nonzero word rounds down, and a shift by at least \(w\) positions returns zero. Branching and memory addressing also cost one operation. The program has only finitely many rational real constants and no oracle or advice. Real values cannot be converted into integer addresses by a floor or arbitrary bit-extraction operation; comparisons can affect the finite control. All input processing, construction of auxiliary data and writing of the output are included in \(T(n)\). There is no randomness. The bound is worst-case over coordinates, degeneracies, number of holes, endpoints and all other valid inputs of size \(n\). This explicitly fixes a deterministic, exact-arithmetic real-RAM interpretation; it is not a bound on the bit complexity of rational coordinates.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof that such a uniform algorithm exists, including exact path feasibility, minimum link count and the stated worst-case little-o operation bound, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of this proposition. A conditional lower bound, an approximation to the minimum number of links, a bound for a restricted direction set, or an algorithm only for polygons without holes does not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: TOPP Problem 22 asks for a subquadratic algorithm for a minimum-link path among planar polygonal obstacles. Its entry is dated 2 August 2001. This card interprets subquadratic as little-o of the square of the input boundary size and makes the deterministic worst-case real-RAM convention explicit.

Mitchell, Rote and Woeginger give an exact algorithm in \(O(E\alpha(n)\log^2 n)\) time, where \(E\) is the number of visibility-graph edges and \(\alpha\) is the inverse Ackermann function. Since \(E=O(n^2)\), this is nearly quadratic in the worst case. Their free space is closed, permits holes and may be unbounded.

Mitchell, Polishchuk and Sysikaski prove that exact link distance with unrestricted directions is 3SUM-hard, even for rectilinear obstacle boundaries. This is a reduction-based result, not an unconditional impossibility theorem. The rectilinear boundaries do not restrict path directions.

The distinction between little-o and a fixed power saving matters: Grønlund and Pettie gave deterministic algorithms for real-number 3SUM whose operation counts are already little-o of the input size squared. Their result is about 3SUM, and is not itself an algorithm for minimum-link paths. The older 3SUM-hardness result therefore does not refute the present little-o target.

The 2014 minimum-link paper also obtains an \(O(\sqrt{h})\)-approximation in subquadratic time, where \(h\) is the number of holes. The May 2025 Dagstuhl seminar report still asks for a better subquadratic approximation. These approximation results and questions do not establish an exact subquadratic algorithm.

The 2016 complexity study separates unrestricted planar bends from bends constrained to polygon boundaries, and from three-dimensional paths. Its NP-hardness results for boundary-reflection paths and three-dimensional paths concern different targets. The paper also explains why real-RAM operation counts and coordinate bit complexity must be distinguished.

checked_sources: Read live TOPP Problem 22 and its revision metadata (2 August 2001). Its short question does not formally distinguish little-o from fixed-power savings or give a detailed machine model; these are explicitly identified editorial conventions.

Downloaded the December 1990 MRW manuscript corresponding to Algorithmica 1992. Visually rendered and read PDF pages 2–4 because pdftotext has broken font encoding. Page 2 gives O(E alpha(n) log²n); pages 3–4 explicitly allow unbounded domains, assume boundedness only for exposition, make free space closed, allow paths on obstacle boundaries and explain why s,t may be regarded as vertices only without loss of generality.

Read Mitchell–Polishchuk–Sysikaski arXiv 1302.3091v1 Introduction, Theorem 2.1 and its reduction proof, Corollary 2.2, Section 2.1 and Theorem 2.7. Their statement that hardness answers TOPP22 was not promoted into an unconditional refutation of the original question.

Read Grønlund–Pettie arXiv 1404.0799v3, posted 30 May 2014, abstract and Theorem 1.1 on PDF page 5. Deterministic real-3SUM time O(n²/(log n/loglog n)^(2/3)) is little-o of n². This primary result supports the distinction between literal subquadratic and truly subquadratic; it does not supply a minimum-link algorithm. Earlier cached v1 has a different loglog power and an anomalous internal compilation date, so the actual revised v3 is the reference used.

Read Kostitsyna–Löffler–Polishchuk–Staals arXiv 1603.06972v1 Section 1.1 Definition 1 and Constraints, Section 1.2 Representation and Computation, Table 1 and the bit-complexity statements in Section2. The full planar unrestricted target is MinLinkPath_{2,2}; boundary-bend (1,2) and three-dimensional variants were not conflated with it. No independent audit of all theorem proofs was performed.

Read the 2025 Dagstuhl report Section 5.11.1 and 5.11.2. The former states the exact planar problem is 3SUM-hard and records subquadratic O(sqrt(n)) approximation; the latter explicitly reports sketches, not a completed exact resolution.

Bounded primary-source searches through 16 September 2026 using minimum-link, exact, subquadratic, logarithmic savings and newer-year terms found no matching exact o(n²) algorithm or unconditional refutation for the full planar model. Rectilinear paths, simple polygons, visibility-query variants, polygon fencing and the 2026 minimum-link measure for bipartite matching were excluded as distinct targets. Search absence is not an exhaustive openness certificate.
